supremeCourt.name: Corte Suprema de Chile
supremeCourt.appointmentMethod: Justices proposed by the Court itself, chosen by the President, and confirmed by 2/3 of the Senate.
supremeCourt.fspEraChanges: No court-packing by left governments. Judicial appointments followed the regular mechanism. Two constituent processes (2021–2023) to replace the 1980 constitution both failed at referendum, leaving the judiciary’s structure unchanged.
supremeCourt.stillServing: The 21-member court is independent; no FSP-driven structural change — a contrast case. Members are not itemized here.

courtHistory.event: The Corte Suprema dates to the 19th century; during the 1973–1990 Pinochet dictatorship the court was widely criticised for acquiescing to the regime, and the 1980 Constitution shaped its design.
A transition-era reform enlarged the court to 21 members and set the mixed appointment mechanism (Court proposes, President chooses, Senate confirms by 2/3).

Across the Socialist/left governments (Lagos, Bachelet, Boric) there was NO court-packing; appointments followed the regular mechanism. The 2021–2023 constituent processes to replace the 1980 Constitution both failed at referendum, leaving the judiciary's structure unchanged.

supremeCourt.justicesNote: Twenty-one justices appointed via the mixed mechanism; individual members are not itemized here.

fspParties.note: Chile's FSP members are the Partido Socialista (PS) and the Partido Comunista (PCCh); the Forum's own roster also lists smaller groups (Izquierda Ciudadana, Partido Humanista, MIR). Crucially, these parties have always governed as a minority faction inside broad center-left coalitions — the Concertación (1990–2010, led by the non-FSP Christian Democrats), the Nueva Mayoría (which added the PCCh from 2013), and Boric's Apruebo Dignidad (2022–, Frente Amplio + PCCh). The PS and PCCh have never commanded a congressional majority on their own, which is why a detailed FSP-bloc seat table is deferred: it would misrepresent their role without a full mapping of each multi-party coalition. Boric's government has notably lacked a majority in either chamber.

legislativeControl.seats: The PS was a junior partner in the Christian-Democrat-led Concertación that governed after the return to democracy; the coalition held working majorities but the FSP parties were a minority within it.
PS presidents Lagos and Bachelet led Concertación governments; the coalition majority rested on non-FSP partners (Christian Democrats, PPD, Radicals) alongside the PS.
Under the right-wing Piñera government the FSP parties sat in opposition.
Bachelet's Nueva Mayoría (Concertación plus the Communist Party) governed with a congressional majority; the FSP parties were part of, but not the whole of, that bloc.
Opposition again under the second Piñera government.

Boric's government (Frente Amplio + the Communist Party) holds the presidency but no majority in either the highly fragmented Chamber (155) or Senate (50), and depends on case-by-case deals with the centre-left and centre.
Under Kast's right-wing government the PS and PCCh sit in opposition; a sourced seat table for the November 2025 congressional election is still to be added.
